title: what the Rig Veda is
hook: a friend's replies go cold, and nobody will say why. In one Rig Veda hymn, the poet Vasishtha asks Varuna straight out: what did I do?

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the Rig Veda is: many gods, and one verse saying what is one, the wise speak of in many ways.

The messages used to come every day. Jokes, photos, long voice notes. Now a friend answers in one word, or not at all. Something happened, but what? You scroll back looking for the moment it changed. You ask a mutual friend, carefully. They shrug: seems like they're upset with you. So there's one honest move left, and it's the hardest: go to the friend and ask, what did I do? A Rig Veda poet makes exactly that move, and the one he asks is a god.
screen: `THE MESSAGES GO QUIET.` → `SEEMS LIKE THEY'RE UPSET.` → `WHAT DID I DO?`

segments.voice: The god is Varuna. In the hymns, Varuna keeps rita, the right order of things, and he sees what people do. The poet is Vasishtha, a seer tradition remembers as the voice of these hymns. Something has gone wrong between them. In paraphrase, Vasishtha says: I ask about this wrong, Varuna, wanting to understand. I go to the wise to ask, and the sages all tell me the same thing: Varuna is angry with you. So he turns to Varuna himself. What was my great offense, he asks, that you would strike the friend who sings your praise? Tell me, and I'll come to you quickly, bowing, free of it. He asks to be released from the wrongs of his fathers, and from the ones he did himself. Then a startling line. It wasn't my own will, Varuna. It was drink, anger, the dice, thoughtlessness. The older one leads the younger astray. Even sleep doesn't keep wrongdoing away. Some readers hear an excuse in that. Others hear a man naming his weak spots out loud: strong drink, a temper, gambling, not thinking. Either way, he doesn't hide them. He brings them to the one he has wronged, and asks to be set right.
screen: `VARUNA SEES WHAT PEOPLE DO.` · `THE SAGES SAY: HE'S ANGRY.` · `WHAT WAS MY OFFENSE?` · `DRINK, ANGER, DICE, CARELESSNESS.`

segments.voice: Let one strained relationship come to mind, at home, at work, anywhere, and instead of arguing your side, ask quietly: what part of this might be mine? If something comes, name it plainly, the way Vasishtha named drink and anger and dice, with no punishment, just honesty; if you pray, you can bring that honesty to God in your own words.
What the Rig Veda is. Not only hymns of praise, but a seer asking Varuna what he did wrong, and naming his own weak spots out loud.
screen: `WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what the Rig Veda is. Even a seer could ask a god, what did I do? Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven, done.

screen: `DAY 1247 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS.`

howItsDone: Hymns to Varuna are read in Hindu tradition as prayers for release from wrongdoing, and the theme of asking forgiveness for faults, known and unknown, appears in prayers and rites of atonement.
